questions.q: What does the doctrine of stare decisis require?
choices: Statutes must always be interpreted literally
Courts follow earlier decisions on substantially the same facts
Judges may decide each case purely on fairness
Appeal courts must rehear all the evidence
questions.explain: Stare decisis ("let the former decision stand") means courts follow precedent when the facts are substantially the same. It gives the law predictability and certainty.

questions.q: A judge decides an earlier case is not binding because one crucial fact is different. What is the judge doing?
choices: Overruling the case
Appealing the case
Distinguishing the case
Adopting the case
questions.explain: "Distinguishing" is the technical term for treating a precedent as inapplicable because a material fact differs.

questions.q: How does a BC court treat a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal?
choices: Binding on all BC courts
Binding on BC trial courts only
Persuasive but not binding
Irrelevant, because it's from another province
questions.explain: A provincial Court of Appeal binds the lower courts of its own province. Elsewhere its decisions are persuasive only.

questions.q: An English decision is directly on point and no Canadian court has ruled on the issue. What is its status in BC?
choices: Binding, because Canadian law came from England
Persuasive, but not binding until adopted by a Canadian court
Binding only in the BC Court of Appeal
It can't be considered at all
questions.explain: English and Commonwealth decisions can be referred to, but they aren't binding until a Canadian court adopts them.

questions.q: When a principle of common law conflicts with a principle of equity, which prevails?
choices: Common law
Equity
Whichever is older
The judge must refer the question to the legislature
questions.explain: Since the Judicature Acts fused the two systems, judges apply both, and where they conflict, equity takes priority.

questions.q: A seller refuses to complete and the buyer wants a court order forcing the transfer of the property. What remedy is this?
choices: Damages
Specific performance
Garnishment
Execution
questions.explain: Specific performance is an equitable remedy ordering the defaulting party to carry out the contract. It's common in real estate because land is treated as unique.

questions.q: A buyer with a strong case for specific performance waits a long time before suing. What's the risk?
choices: None, as long as she's within the 2-year limitation period
The court may refuse the equitable remedy because of the delay
The case automatically moves to Small Claims Court
She loses the right to damages as well
questions.explain: Equitable remedies are discretionary. Even within the legal limitation period, unreasonable delay can cost you equitable relief. You need "fast feet".

questions.q: Where do BC municipalities get their power to pass bylaws?
choices: Directly from the Constitution
From powers delegated by the federal government
From powers carved out of provincial power
From the common law
questions.explain: Municipalities have no constitutional standing of their own. The province hands them specific powers, such as zoning and building bylaws.

questions.q: Which level of government holds the residual power over matters the Constitution doesn't specifically assign?
choices: Federal
Provincial
Municipal
It's shared equally
questions.explain: The residual power to legislate over unassigned areas is federal.

questions.q: Why is almost all real estate law in BC provincial?
choices: Because the federal government delegated it in 1990
Because the Constitution gives the provinces jurisdiction over property and civil rights
Because municipalities asked for it
Because real estate is a criminal law matter
questions.explain: "Property and civil rights" is a provincial head of power, which is why RESA, the Land Title Act and the Strata Property Act are all provincial statutes.

questions.q: Before the Real Estate Services Act, did a person acting as a real estate agent need a licence at common law?
choices: Yes, the common law always required a licence
No. The licensing requirement was created by statute
Only for commercial transactions
Only in Vancouver
questions.explain: This is the course's own example of statute changing the common law: the common law had no licensing requirement, and RESA created one.

questions.q: Which of these is a public law matter?
choices: A tenant suing a landlord for an unreturned deposit
A buyer suing for breach of contract
A prosecution for fraud
A negligence claim against a licensee
questions.explain: Criminal law is public law: the state is a party. The other three are private (civil) disputes between individuals.

questions.q: Under BC's estates system, who holds the underlying title to all land?
choices: The registered fee simple owner
The municipality
The Crown
The Land Title Office
questions.explain: BC still rests on the feudal estates system: the Crown holds underlying title, and a fee simple owner holds the largest estate available under it.
questions.ref: Lesson 1 · Why you don't actually own your land

questions.q: A strata corporation is owed $85,000 in unpaid strata fees. Can the Civil Resolution Tribunal hear the claim?
choices: No, the CRT's limit is $5,000
No, the CRT's limit is $35,000
Yes. Strata disputes have no monetary limit at the CRT
Only if the owner agrees
questions.explain: The CRT can decide most strata disputes with no monetary limit. The $5,000 cap applies only to its small claims category.

questions.q: Someone files a $7,500 small claim at the CRT. What happens to the $2,500 above the CRT's limit?
choices: It's transferred to Small Claims Court
It must be abandoned and can't be claimed anywhere else
It's added to the next claim
The CRT can award it at its discretion
questions.explain: You may file above $5,000 at the CRT, but the excess is given up permanently.

questions.q: How long does a party have to seek judicial review of a CRT final decision in the BC Supreme Court?
choices: 14 days
30 days
60 days
2 years
questions.explain: Judicial review of a CRT final decision must be sought within 60 days.

questions.q: A buyer wants to sue for $28,000 and no arbitration clause applies. Which court fits the claim?
choices: Civil Resolution Tribunal
Small Claims Court
BC Court of Appeal
Supreme Court of Canada
questions.explain: Small Claims Court hears most claims from $5,001 to $35,000 (subject to its territorial limit). Above $35,000, go to the BC Supreme Court or reduce the claim.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a trial court and an appeal court?
choices: Appeal courts hear new witnesses
Trial courts decide the facts; appeal courts review the legal principles applied
Appeal courts only hear criminal cases
Trial courts always sit with three judges
questions.explain: Trial courts hear the evidence and find the facts. Appeal courts generally don't rehear evidence. They look for errors in how the law was applied.

questions.q: When might the BC Court of Appeal sit with five judges instead of three?
choices: When the claim is over $1 million
When an important precedent may be overturned
When the appeal comes from Small Claims Court
When a jury was used at trial
questions.explain: The usual panel is three judges, but five may sit where an important precedent may be overturned.

questions.q: A party applies for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and the Court declines to hear it. What happens?
choices: The case goes back for a new trial
The BC Court of Appeal's decision stands
The appeal is heard by the BC Supreme Court instead
The original trial decision is restored
questions.explain: Unlike the BC Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court of Canada chooses which appeals it hears. If it refuses, the Court of Appeal's decision stands.

questions.q: At trial, the judge finds the plaintiff's and defendant's versions of events equally likely. What is the result?
choices: The plaintiff wins half the claim
A new trial is ordered
The claim is dismissed
The judge sends it to mediation
questions.explain: The plaintiff bears the burden of proving the case on a balance of probabilities (more likely than not). A tie means the burden wasn't met.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the pleadings stage?
choices: To let the judge hear witnesses early
To narrow and define the issues the court needs to decide
To calculate court costs
To choose a jury
questions.explain: Pleadings (notice of civil claim, response, reply, counterclaim) set out each side's position so the real points in dispute are clear.

questions.q: Which statement about court costs is correct?
choices: They equal the winner's full legal fees
They are set by a tariff, cover only part of legal expenses, and are at the court's discretion
They are always paid by the plaintiff
They're only awarded in Small Claims Court
questions.explain: Costs are not legal fees. They follow a tariff in the court rules, partially reimburse the winner, discourage weak cases, and are discretionary.

questions.q: A sheriff can't find any assets to seize under a writ of execution. How is the writ returned?
choices: Marked nulla bona
Marked res judicata
Marked stare decisis
Marked ultra vires
questions.explain: Nulla bona means "no goods". It records that there was nothing to seize.

questions.q: A judgment creditor registers the judgment against the debtor's land. How often must the registration be renewed?
choices: Every year
Every second year
Every five years
Never
questions.explain: A registered judgment must be renewed every second year to remain valid.

questions.q: Under a garnishing order against wages, what portion of a debtor's wages is generally exempt?
choices: 100% if the debtor has dependants
questions.explain: 70% of wages are exempt, and never less than $100/month (single) or $200/month (married with dependants). The exemption doesn't apply to debts for lodging.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a mediator and an arbitrator?
choices: A mediator decides the dispute; an arbitrator only advises
A mediator helps the parties reach their own agreement; an arbitrator makes a binding decision
Only arbitration is private
Mediation is only used for criminal cases
questions.explain: A mediator helps you agree. An arbitrator tells you the answer, in an award that is usually binding and final.

questions.q: In a BC Supreme Court action, who can require all the parties to attend mediation under the Notice to Mediate (General) Regulation?
choices: Only the judge
Only the plaintiff
Any one party to the action
All parties must agree first
questions.explain: Any single party can deliver a Notice to Mediate and require the others to participate. Refusing can lead to court sanctions.
questions.ref: Lesson 1 · Mediation can be forced on you

questions.q: Under BC's Limitation Act, when does the basic 2-year limitation period usually start?
choices: On the date of the wrongful act
On the date the claim is discovered
On the date a lawyer is hired
On January 1 of the following year
questions.explain: The basic period runs from discovery: when the claimant knew or reasonably ought to have known of the loss, that the defendant caused it, and that court was an appropriate remedy.

questions.q: What is the length of the ultimate limitation period?
choices: 2 years
6 years
15 years
30 years
questions.explain: The ultimate limitation period was reduced from 30 to 15 years and usually runs from the day of the act or omission.

questions.q: A defendant makes a partial payment on a fixed-sum claim. What effect can that have?
choices: None
It ends the claim
It restarts both limitation periods from the date of payment
It extends the basic period by 6 months only
questions.explain: Acknowledging liability, by partial payment or written confirmation, restarts both the basic and ultimate limitation periods.

questions.q: A registered letter arrives at the brokerage addressed to another licensee who's out. What should you do?
choices: Sign for it so it isn't returned
Sign and email them a photo
Not sign. Only the named recipient should sign for registered mail
Sign using the managing broker's name
questions.explain: The signature is proof of receipt and can start court deadlines running. Only the person it's addressed to should sign.

questions.q: A client complains about something you're sure has no merit. Do you need to notify the E&O insurer?
choices: No, only if a lawsuit is filed
No, only if your managing broker agrees it has merit
Yes, in writing as soon as practicable, for any circumstance that could reasonably lead to a claim, however unmeritorious
Only if the amount is over $5,000
questions.explain: Notice is a condition of coverage, and it's triggered by the possibility of a claim, not your opinion of its merit.
